text.title: Agency Pricing Tiers Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every Agency Pricing Tiers application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The rate sheet MUST present exactly three priced tiers in the order good, better, best. A fourth priced tier MUST NOT be added; an unpriced "custom" option may exist only outside the three-tier table.

rationale.source: Rafi Mohammed, 'The Good-Better-Best Approach to Pricing', Harvard Business Review (2018); Dan Ariely, Predictably Irrational (2008), the decoy effect

rule.rationale: Three options let the buyer compare rather than decide yes/no; a fourth splits the anchor and the middle stops being the obvious choice. Agencies that add "enterprise" as a fourth priced row find the third tier stops selling.

rule.statement: Gross margin per tier MUST be computed as price minus delivery cost (estimated hours × loaded hourly cost plus pass-through costs) and recorded on the playbook step. The best tier MUST have the highest gross margin in both absolute currency and percentage; if it does not, the tier scopes or prices MUST be revised before publication.

rationale.source: Blair Enns, Pricing Creativity (2018); AGENTS.md scope: best is the actual margin tier

rule.rationale: The common failure is a best tier stuffed with every deliverable the team could think of, so it wins on revenue and loses on margin: each best-tier sale then costs the agency its most senior hours at the lowest effective rate.

rule.statement: Tier prices MUST follow the 3 / 5 / 8 relative multiplier within 15 percent: better is roughly 1.67× good and best roughly 1.6× better. A gap outside that band MUST be justified in the step's `exit_criterion` by a named scope difference, not by "what the market pays".

rationale.source: AGENTS.md scope: mid-tier anchoring through 3/5/8 price gap distribution; Madhavan Ramanujam and Georg Tacke, Monetizing Innovation (2016), on good-better-best gaps

rule.rationale: Equal steps (1x / 2x / 3x) make the top tier look like the middle tier plus a surcharge; a top tier at 4x the middle reads as a different product and stops anchoring. The 3/5/8 shape keeps the best tier close enough to lift the perceived value of the middle.

rule.statement: Every deliverable in good MUST appear in better, and every deliverable in better MUST appear in best, with equal or greater quantity and equal or faster turnaround. Each tier MUST list deliverables with quantities and turnaround times; a tier that swaps a deliverable out instead of adding MUST be rejected.

rationale.source: Rafi Mohammed, HBR (2018); widely established packaging practice

rule.rationale: A buyer who has to give something up to move up a tier stops moving. Nested tiers also make the scope-up conversation a single sentence: "you already have everything in better; best adds these three items".

rule.statement: The good tier MUST omit at least one deliverable that the agency's ICP needs to reach its stated outcome (the fence), and that omission MUST be named on the rate sheet. The better tier MUST contain the complete core deliverable for the ICP and MUST be the tier the sales script recommends by default.

rationale.source: Rafi Mohammed, HBR (2018), on fencing the good tier; Blair Enns, Pricing Creativity (2018)

rule.rationale: Without a fence, price-sensitive buyers who could afford better take good and the middle tier never sells. With the fence and a complete middle, good becomes the entry for buyers who genuinely do not need the omitted piece, and the rest migrate up on their own.

rule.statement: The playbook step MUST document the mid-engagement scope-up: the trigger (a request outside the current tier's deliverable list), the price (the difference between the two tier prices, pro-rated to the remaining term), who at the agency approves it, and the written confirmation required from the client before work starts. Scope-up as free goodwill MUST NOT be permitted.

rationale.source: AGENTS.md scope: scope-up procedure mid-engagement documented; widely established agency account-management practice

rule.rationale: Unpriced extras are how the good tier's margin quietly falls to zero. A written procedure turns every out-of-scope request into either an upgrade or a polite no, and gives the account manager a sentence to say.

rule.statement: A concession MUST be delivered by removing a named deliverable or quantity from the tier, never by lowering the tier's published price. The published tier prices MUST NOT vary by client; a client-specific price MUST be presented as a custom scope with its own deliverable list.

rationale.source: Blair Enns, Pricing Creativity (2018); Madhavan Ramanujam and Georg Tacke, Monetizing Innovation (2016)

rule.rationale: A price discount on better collapses the gap to good and destroys the anchor for every future proposal that client, or their referrals, will see. Trading scope keeps the price ladder intact and the margin rule true.

rule.statement: Proposals and the rate sheet MUST list the best tier first, then better, then good, with the price visible on every tier. A proposal that leads with good, or hides best behind "contact us", MUST be revised.

rationale.source: Blair Enns, Pricing Creativity (2018), on anchoring high; Dan Ariely, Predictably Irrational (2008)

rule.rationale: The first number the buyer reads becomes the reference point. Leading with good anchors the conversation at the cheapest option and every later tier is then read as an upsell rather than as the standard.
